analysis.one_liner: Requires nursing homes to have a registered nurse on duty around the clock.
analysis.headline: The bill to require a registered nurse in every nursing home 24/7 was referred to two House committees and never received a hearing, a vote, or further action before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Current law lets nursing homes that serve Medicare and Medicaid patients skip having a registered nurse on duty, using a waiver. This bill would close that loophole: every nursing home and skilled nursing facility would have to have at least one registered nurse on site 24 hours a day, 7 days a week, to assess residents, watch for changes in their condition, and provide direct care. The rule would take effect one year after enactment. The bill was sent to two House committees in February 2015 and never moved again.
analysis.who_benefits: Nursing home and skilled nursing facility residents and their families gain a guarantee that a registered nurse — the most highly trained caregiver on staff — is present at all times to catch medical problems, supervise care, and respond to emergencies. Residents on Medicaid, who tend to be the poorest and sickest, would benefit most, since the requirement applies to facilities receiving Medicaid money.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Nursing home residents and their families

how_it_helps.text: The bill removes the statutory waiver that lets nursing homes operate without a registered nurse for stretches of time, instead requiring at least one registered professional nurse on duty 24 hours a day, 7 days a week, in both Medicare skilled nursing facilities and Medicaid nursing facilities.

The on-duty RN must provide assessment, surveillance, and direct care to residents around the clock — meaning ongoing monitoring of residents' conditions for clinical decisionmaking, not just nominal coverage.
The new rule applies to payments for services furnished starting one year after enactment, giving facilities time to hire.

analysis.who_pays: Nursing homes would bear the cost of hiring registered nurses to fill round-the-clock shifts, which could run into the hundreds of millions of dollars industry-wide and would likely be passed along to facility budgets. Some of that cost could be offset through higher Medicare and Medicaid payment rates, which taxpayers fund; some facilities in rural or low-income areas might have trouble finding nurses to hire.
analysis.who_pays_short: Nursing home operators, and taxpayers partly

drawbacks.text: The mandate creates a real cost for nursing home operators, who must staff a registered nurse on every shift including nights and weekends; facilities that cannot absorb the expense could face financial strain, and some observers of the long-term care industry have historically argued such requirements could force marginal facilities to close.

One RN per facility is a modest standard — it does not set an overall minimum ratio of nurses to residents, so a large home with many residents would still have only one registered nurse on duty at a time.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit — a trained nurse always present to detect a fall, an infection, or a medication error — is significant for some of the most vulnerable people in the country, and the one-year phase-in is a reasonable concession to operators. The bill is a floor rather than a full fix: one RN in a large facility is thin coverage, and the cost falls substantially on operators who would seek higher public reimbursement. Still, the loophole it closes is real and the burden it imposes is squarely on facilities paid to provide safe care.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee and the Energy and Commerce Committee in February 2015, then to the health subcommittee, and never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the 114th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Jan Schakowsky introduced the bill on February 12, 2015 with five original cosponsors.
It was referred to the Committee on Ways and Means and, in addition, to the Committee on Energy and Commerce for provisions within their jurisdiction.
In mid-February 2015 it was referred to the Subcommittee on Health in each committee, where it sat without further action.
Fourteen House members cosponsored the bill, all Democrats, and no further action was taken before the Congress ended on January 3, 2017.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Nursing home operators are better off because the bill died: they avoided a requirement to staff a registered nurse around the clock, with no compensating change to their payment rates or obligations.

against.name: American Health Care Association and nursing home operators
against.what_they_did: The long-term care industry has consistently opposed mandatory registered nurse staffing minimums as a costly mandate on facilities; no industry activity on this bill appears in the congressional record.

sides.party_line_note: All 6 original sponsors and all 14 cosponsors were House Democrats; no Republican supported the bill, and the Republican-controlled committees took no action on it.

industries.industry: Nursing homes and skilled nursing facilities
industries.note: The bill requires these facilities to hire at least one registered nurse for every hour of the week, a direct labor cost they currently avoid through a statutory waiver. Their interest in defeating the mandate ran against residents' interest in having a nurse present.
A 24/7 RN requirement would create nursing jobs and raise demand for licensed nurses, aligning with the public interest in better care.
